questions.question: A binary composition $*$ is defined in $\mathbb{Z}^{+}$ by $a*b=a^{b}-a$; $a,b\in\mathbb{Z}^{+}$.
questions.answer:
**The definition.** For positive integers $a,b$,

$$a*b=a^{b}-a$$

*Note on the paper:* in the scanned copy this question stops after the definition — the actual demand (evaluate a particular product, or test commutativity/associativity) is cut off at the printed margin. The booklet's own solution likewise only restates $a*b=a^{b}-a$.

**What such a question asks, worked out:**

The standard demands are all answerable from the definition.

**Evaluate:** $2*3=2^{3}-2=8-2=6$; $3*2=3^{2}-3=9-3=6$. (These two happen to agree.) But $2*4=2^{4}-2=14$ while $4*2=4^{2}-4=12$, so $2*4\ne4*2$.

**Commutativity:** $a*b=b*a$ would require $a^{b}-a=b^{a}-b$ for all $a,b\in\mathbb{Z}^{+}$, which fails already at $(a,b)=(2,4)$. So $*$ is **not commutative**.

**Associativity:** $(a*b)*c=a^{b^{c}}-a^{b}$ whereas $a*(b*c)=a^{b^{c}-b}-a$; these differ (e.g. $a=2,b=3,c=2$: LHS $=2^{9}-8=504$, RHS $=2^{6}-2=62$). So $*$ is **not associative** either.

questions.question: Evaluate: $\cos^{-1}\left(\cos\dfrac{13\pi}{6}\right)$.
questions.answer:
$\cos^{-1}(\cos\theta)=\theta$ only when $\theta\in[0,\pi]$; here $\dfrac{13\pi}{6}>\pi$, so first reduce the angle.

$$\frac{13\pi}{6}=2\pi+\frac{\pi}{6}$$

Cosine has period $2\pi$, so

$$\cos\frac{13\pi}{6}=\cos\left(2\pi+\frac{\pi}{6}\right)=\cos\frac{\pi}{6}$$

Now $\dfrac{\pi}{6}\in[0,\pi]$, so taking $\cos^{-1}$ is safe:

$$\cos^{-1}\left(\cos\frac{13\pi}{6}\right)=\cos^{-1}\left(\cos\frac{\pi}{6}\right)=\frac{\pi}{6}$$

**Answer: $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$.** (Numerically $\cos\frac{13\pi}{6}=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}=0.866$, whose principal arccosine is $\frac{\pi}{6}$ ✓.)

questions.question: Construct a $3\times2$ matrix whose $(i,j)^{th}$ element is $a_{ij}=\dfrac12|i-3j|$.
questions.answer:
A $3\times2$ matrix has $i=1,2,3$ (rows) and $j=1,2$ (columns):

$$A=\begin{bmatrix}a_{11}&a_{12}\\ a_{21}&a_{22}\\ a_{31}&a_{32}\end{bmatrix},\qquad a_{ij}=\frac12|i-3j|$$

Compute each entry:

$$a_{11}=\tfrac12|1-3|=\tfrac12(2)=1,\qquad a_{12}=\tfrac12|1-6|=\tfrac12(5)=\frac52$$

$$a_{21}=\tfrac12|2-3|=\tfrac12(1)=\frac12,\qquad a_{22}=\tfrac12|2-6|=\tfrac12(4)=2$$

$$a_{31}=\tfrac12|3-3|=0,\qquad a_{32}=\tfrac12|3-6|=\tfrac12(3)=\frac32$$

$$\therefore\ A=\begin{bmatrix}1&\frac52\\ \frac12&2\\ 0&\frac32\end{bmatrix}$$

All entries are non-negative because of the modulus, and the entries grow away from the diagonal $i=3j$ where $a_{ij}=0$.

questions.question: If $A=\begin{bmatrix}2&-1\\0&3\end{bmatrix}$, then find $A^{2}$.
questions.answer:
$$A^{2}=A\cdot A=\begin{bmatrix}2&-1\\0&3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2&-1\\0&3\end{bmatrix}$$

Multiply row-by-column:

$$(1,1):\ (2)(2)+(-1)(0)=4\qquad (1,2):\ (2)(-1)+(-1)(3)=-5$$

$$(2,1):\ (0)(2)+(3)(0)=0\qquad (2,2):\ (0)(-1)+(3)(3)=9$$

$$\therefore\ A^{2}=\begin{bmatrix}4&-5\\0&9\end{bmatrix}$$

(Square of an upper-triangular matrix stays upper triangular, with the diagonal entries squared: $2^2=4$ and $3^2=9$ ✓.)

questions.question: Without expanding, prove that $\begin{vmatrix}x+y&y+z&z+x\\ z&x&y\\ 1&1&1\end{vmatrix}=0$.
questions.answer:
Let the given determinant be $\Delta$. Apply the row operation $R_1\to R_1+R_2$, which does not change a determinant:

$$\Delta=\begin{vmatrix}x+y+z&x+y+z&x+y+z\\ z&x&y\\ 1&1&1\end{vmatrix}$$

The first row is now entirely $(x+y+z)$; take it out as a factor:

$$\Delta=(x+y+z)\begin{vmatrix}1&1&1\\ z&x&y\\ 1&1&1\end{vmatrix}$$

The first and third rows are identical. A determinant with two identical rows is zero (swapping them would change the sign while leaving the determinant unchanged, forcing $\Delta=-\Delta$):

$$\therefore\ \Delta=(x+y+z)\cdot0=0\qquad\blacksquare$$

*(Check by direct expansion for $x=1,y=2,z=3$: the determinant of $\begin{bmatrix}3&5&4\\3&1&2\\1&1&1\end{bmatrix}$ is $3(1-2)-5(3-2)+4(3-1)=-3-5+8=0$ ✓.)*

questions.question: Find the slope of the tangent to the curve $y=x^{2}-2$ at $x=2$.
questions.answer:
The slope of the tangent at a point is $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ evaluated there. For $y=x^2-2$:

$$\frac{dy}{dx}=2x$$

At $x=2$:

$$\left.\frac{dy}{dx}\right|_{x=2}=2(2)=4$$

**The slope of the tangent is 4.** (The point of contact is $(2,\,2)$, and the tangent line is $y-2=4(x-2)$, i.e. $y=4x-6$.)

questions.question: Evaluate: $\displaystyle\int\frac{\tan^{-1}x}{1+x^{2}}\,dx$.
questions.answer:
Put $t=\tan^{-1}x$. Then

$$\frac{dt}{dx}=\frac{1}{1+x^{2}}\ \Rightarrow\ dt=\frac{dx}{1+x^{2}}$$

The whole integrand collapses to $t\,dt$:

$$I=\int t\,dt=\frac{t^{2}}{2}+C$$

Substituting back $t=\tan^{-1}x$:

$$\therefore\ \int\frac{\tan^{-1}x}{1+x^{2}}dx=\frac{\left(\tan^{-1}x\right)^{2}}{2}+C$$

Check by differentiating: $\dfrac{d}{dx}\cdot\dfrac{(\tan^{-1}x)^2}{2}=(\tan^{-1}x)\cdot\dfrac{1}{1+x^2}$ ✓ — exactly the integrand.

questions.question: Find the value of $\hat i\cdot(\hat j\times\hat k)+\hat j\cdot(\hat k\times\hat i)+\hat k\cdot(\hat i\times\hat j)$.
questions.answer:
Use the cyclic cross products of the unit vectors:

$$\hat j\times\hat k=\hat i,\qquad \hat k\times\hat i=\hat j,\qquad \hat i\times\hat j=\hat k$$

Substituting:

$$\hat i\cdot\hat i+\hat j\cdot\hat j+\hat k\cdot\hat k$$

and since $\hat i\cdot\hat i=\hat j\cdot\hat j=\hat k\cdot\hat k=1$:

$$=1+1+1=3$$

**The value is 3.** (Each term is a scalar triple product $[\hat i,\hat j,\hat k]=1$ — the volume of the unit cube — so the sum is $3$.)

questions.question: Find the area of a parallelogram whose adjacent sides are the vectors $\vec a=\hat i-2\hat j+3\hat k$ and $\vec b=2\hat i-\hat j+4\hat k$.
questions.answer:
The area of a parallelogram with adjacent sides $\vec a,\vec b$ is $\left|\vec a\times\vec b\right|$.

$$\vec a\times\vec b=\begin{vmatrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\ 1&-2&3\\ 2&-1&4\end{vmatrix}$$

$$=\hat i\left[(-2)(4)-(3)(-1)\right]-\hat j\left[(1)(4)-(3)(2)\right]+\hat k\left[(1)(-1)-(-2)(2)\right]$$

$$=\hat i(-8+3)-\hat j(4-6)+\hat k(-1+4)$$

$$=-5\hat i+2\hat j+3\hat k$$

$$\left|\vec a\times\vec b\right|=\sqrt{(-5)^{2}+2^{2}+3^{2}}=\sqrt{25+4+9}=\sqrt{38}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{Area}=\sqrt{38}\ \text{square units}\approx6.164$$

*Note on the printed key:* the booklet's cross product has the $\hat k$-component as $(4-6)=-2$ and concludes $\sqrt{25+4+4}=\sqrt{33}$. Recomputing, the $\hat k$-component is $(1)(-1)-(-2)(2)=-1+4=3$, so the magnitude is $\sqrt{38}$, not $\sqrt{33}$. The area is **$\sqrt{38}$ square units**.

questions.question: Write the Cartesian equations of a straight line passing through the point $(-1,2,0)$ and whose direction ratios are $2,4,-3$.
questions.answer:
A line through $(x_1,y_1,z_1)$ with direction ratios $(a,b,c)$ has Cartesian equations

$$\frac{x-x_1}{a}=\frac{y-y_1}{b}=\frac{z-z_1}{c}$$

With $(x_1,y_1,z_1)=(-1,2,0)$ and $(a,b,c)=(2,4,-3)$:

$$\frac{x+1}{2}=\frac{y-2}{4}=\frac{z-0}{-3}$$

$$\therefore\ \frac{x+1}{2}=\frac{y-2}{4}=\frac{z}{-3}$$

(Equivalently, in parametric form, $x=-1+2t,\ y=2+4t,\ z=-3t$.)

questions.question: Prove that $\tan^{-1}\sqrt x=\dfrac12\cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1-x}{1+x}\right)$.
questions.answer:
Put $\tan^{-1}\sqrt x=\theta$, so that $\theta\in\left[0,\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$ and

$$\tan\theta=\sqrt x\ \Rightarrow\ x=\tan^{2}\theta$$

Now rewrite the right-hand side in terms of $\theta$:

$$\frac{1-x}{1+x}=\frac{1-\tan^{2}\theta}{1+\tan^{2}\theta}$$

Using the identities $1+\tan^2\theta=\sec^2\theta$ and $\cos2\theta=\dfrac{1-\tan^2\theta}{1+\tan^2\theta}$:

$$\frac{1-x}{1+x}=\cos2\theta$$

Therefore

$$\frac12\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{1-x}{1+x}\right)=\frac12\cos^{-1}(\cos2\theta)$$

Since $x\ge0$ gives $\theta\in\left[0,\frac{\pi}{2}\right)$, we have $2\theta\in[0,\pi)$, which is exactly the range of the principal value of $\cos^{-1}$, so $\cos^{-1}(\cos2\theta)=2\theta$:

$$=\frac12(2\theta)=\theta=\tan^{-1}\sqrt x\qquad\blacksquare$$

*(Numerical check: at $x=2$, both sides equal $0.9553$ rad ✓; at $x=7$, both equal $1.2094$ ✓.)*

questions.question: Let $f(x)=x+7$ and $g(x)=x-7$, $x\in R$. Find: (i) $f\circ f(7)$ (ii) $f\circ g(7)$ (iii) $g\circ f(7)$ (iv) $g\circ g(7)$.
questions.answer:
Recall $(f\circ g)(x)=f\left(g(x)\right)$ — the inner function acts first.

**(i) $f\circ f(7)=f\left(f(7)\right)$:**

$$f(7)=7+7=14,\qquad f(14)=14+7=21$$

$$\therefore\ f\circ f(7)=21$$

**(ii) $f\circ g(7)=f\left(g(7)\right)$:**

$$g(7)=7-7=0,\qquad f(0)=0+7=7$$

$$\therefore\ f\circ g(7)=7$$

**(iii) $g\circ f(7)=g\left(f(7)\right)$:**

$$f(7)=14,\qquad g(14)=14-7=7$$

$$\therefore\ g\circ f(7)=7$$

**(iv) $g\circ g(7)=g\left(g(7)\right)$:**

$$g(7)=0,\qquad g(0)=0-7=-7$$

$$\therefore\ g\circ g(7)=-7$$

**Remark.** Here $f$ and $g$ are inverses, so $f\circ g=g\circ f=$ identity, which is why (ii) and (iii) both return $7$.

*Note on the printed key:* the booklet writes $f\circ g(7)=f(0)=0-7=-7$, i.e. it applies $g$ a second time. The correct value is $f(0)=0+7=7$; parts (i), (iii), (iv) as printed are correct.

questions.question: Prove that $\begin{vmatrix}b+c&a-b&a\\ c+a&b-c&b\\ a+b&c-a&c\end{vmatrix}=3abc-a^{3}-b^{3}-c^{3}$.
questions.answer:
Apply column operations — **first** $C_1\to C_1+C_2$, then $C_2\to C_2-C_3$. Neither changes the value.

**Step 1:**

$$\Delta=\begin{vmatrix}a+c&-b&a\\ a+b&-c&b\\ b+c&-a&c\end{vmatrix}$$

**Step 2 ($C_2\to C_2-C_3$):**

$$\Delta=\begin{vmatrix}a+c&-(b+a)&a\\ a+b&-(c+b)&b\\ b+c&-(a+c)&c\end{vmatrix}=-\begin{vmatrix}a+c&a+b&a\\ a+b&b+c&b\\ b+c&c+a&c\end{vmatrix}$$

Expand along the first row:

$$\Delta=(-1)\Big[(a+c)\left((b+c)c-b(c+a)\right)-(a+b)\left((a+b)c-b(b+c)\right)+a\left((a+b)(c+a)-(b+c)^{2}\right)\Big]$$

Evaluating the three brackets:

$$(a+c)\left(bc+c^{2}-bc-ab\right)=(a+c)\left(c^{2}-ab\right)$$

$$-(a+b)\left(ac+bc-b^{2}-bc\right)=-(a+b)\left(ac-b^{2}\right)$$

$$a\left(ac+a^{2}+bc+ab-b^{2}-2bc-c^{2}\right)=a\left(a^{2}+ab-b^{2}-bc+ac-c^{2}\right)$$

Putting these inside $\Delta=(-1)[\ldots]$ and collecting like powers (the $a^2b$, $ab^2$, $abc$-type cross terms all cancel in pairs):

$$\Delta=(-1)\left[c^{3}+a^{3}+b^{3}-3abc\right]$$

$$\therefore\ \Delta=3abc-a^{3}-b^{3}-c^{3}\qquad\blacksquare$$

*(Verified for $(a,b,c)=(4,6,5)$: the determinant is $-45$ and $3abc-a^3-b^3-c^3=360-64-216-125=-45$ ✓; and for $a=b=c$ both sides vanish ✓.)*

questions.question: Find the values of $a$ and $b$ such that the following function may be continuous everywhere: $f(x)=\begin{cases}5 & ;\ x\le2\\ ax+b & ;\ 2<x<10\\ 21 & ;\ x\ge10\end{cases}$
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — here $f$ is continuous.** For a function defined piecewise by polynomials, continuity can only fail at the joining points $x=2$ and $x=10$, where the one-sided limits must agree with the value.

**At $x=2$:**

$$f(2)=5,\qquad \lim_{x\to2^{+}}f(x)=\lim_{x\to2^{+}}(ax+b)=2a+b$$

$$
\lim_{x\to2^{-}}f(x)=5$$

Continuity requires $\lim_{x\to2^{-}}f(x)=\lim_{x\to2^{+}}f(x)=f(2)$:

$$2a+b=5\qquad\ldots(1)$$

**At $x=10$:**

$$f(10)=21,\qquad \lim_{x\to10^{-}}f(x)=\lim_{x\to10^{-}}(ax+b)=10a+b$$

$$
\lim_{x\to10^{+}}f(x)=21$$

$$10a+b=21\qquad\ldots(2)$$

**Step 2 — solve.** Subtract (1) from (2):

$$(10a+b)-(2a+b)=21-5\ \Rightarrow\ 8a=16\ \Rightarrow\ a=2$$

Substituting into (1):

$$2(2)+b=5\ \Rightarrow\ b=5-4=1$$

$$\therefore\ a=2,\quad b=1$$

**Check:** with $a=2,b=1$ the middle piece is $2x+1$, giving $5$ at $x=2$ and $21$ at $x=10$ — both matching the constant pieces, so $f$ is continuous everywhere ✓.

questions.question: Or, if $y=\log\left(\sin\sqrt{x^{2}+1}\right)$, find $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$.
questions.answer:
Three nested functions: log of sine of square root. Differentiate outward-in.

$$\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1}{\sin\sqrt{x^{2}+1}}\cdot\frac{d}{dx}\sin\sqrt{x^{2}+1}$$

$$=\frac{1}{\sin\sqrt{x^{2}+1}}\cdot\cos\sqrt{x^{2}+1}\cdot\frac{d}{dx}\sqrt{x^{2}+1}$$

$$=\cot\sqrt{x^{2}+1}\cdot\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x^{2}+1}}\cdot2x$$

$$\therefore\ \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{x\cot\sqrt{x^{2}+1}}{\sqrt{x^{2}+1}}$$

Equivalently, writing $\dfrac{\cos}{\sin}=\cot$ in the booklet's notation:

$$\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{x\tan\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}-\sqrt{x^{2}+1}\right)}{\sqrt{x^{2}+1}}$$

The compact form $\dfrac{x\cot\sqrt{x^{2}+1}}{\sqrt{x^{2}+1}}$ is the standard answer.

questions.question: If $x=3\sin t-\sin3t$, $y=3\cos t-\cos3t$, find $\dfrac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}$ at $t=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$.
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — first derivatives.**

$$\frac{dx}{dt}=3\cos t-3\cos3t=3(\cos t-\cos3t)$$

$$\frac{dy}{dt}=-3\sin t+3\sin3t=3(\sin3t-\sin t)$$

$$\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{dy/dt}{dx/dt}=\frac{\sin3t-\sin t}{\cos t-\cos3t}$$

Use the sum-to-product formulas $\sin3t-\sin t=2\cos2t\sin t$ and $\cos t-\cos3t=2\sin2t\sin t$:

$$\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{2\cos2t\sin t}{2\sin2t\sin t}=\cot2t$$

**Step 2 — second derivative.** Differentiate $\cot2t$ with respect to $t$, then divide by $\dfrac{dx}{dt}$:

$$\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}=\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(\cot2t)}{dx/dt}=\frac{-2\,\mathrm{cosec}^{2}2t}{3(\cos t-\cos3t)}$$

**Step 3 — evaluate at $t=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$.** Here $2t=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$, so $\sin\dfrac{2\pi}{3}=\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ and $\mathrm{cosec}^{2}\dfrac{2\pi}{3}=\dfrac43$; also $\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3}=\dfrac12$ and $\cos\pi=-1$, so $\cos t-\cos3t=\dfrac12+1=\dfrac32$:

$$\left.\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}\right|_{t=\pi/3}=\frac{-2\left(\frac43\right)}{3\left(\frac32\right)}=\frac{-\frac83}{\frac92}=-\frac{8}{3}\cdot\frac{2}{9}=-\frac{16}{27}$$

$$\therefore\ \left.\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}\right|_{t=\pi/3}=-\frac{16}{27}$$

*(Also $\left.\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right|_{t=\pi/3}=\cot\dfrac{2\pi}{3}=-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}$.)*

*Note on the printed key:* the booklet simplifies $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ to $\tan2t$ (it is $\cot2t$) and then writes $\dfrac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}=\dfrac{2\sec^{2}2t}{3\cos t-3\cos3t}$, dropping the factor $3$ from $dx/dt$; the two slips happen to cancel in their final steps only in their own numbers, and they print $\frac89$. Direct numerical differentiation of the parametric curve gives $-0.59259=-\frac{16}{27}$, so the printed $\frac89$ is incorrect.

questions.question: A balloon which always remains spherical is being inflated by pumping in 900 cubic centimetres of gas per second. Find the rate at which the radius of the balloon is increasing when the radius is 15 cm.
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — set up.** Let $r$ be the radius and $V$ the volume at time $t$. The balloon is spherical, so

$$V=\frac43\pi r^{3}$$

Given: $\dfrac{dV}{dt}=900\ \text{cm}^3/\text{s}$. Required: $\dfrac{dr}{dt}$ when $r=15$.

**Step 2 — relate the rates** by differentiating with respect to $t$ (chain rule):

$$\frac{dV}{dt}=\frac{dV}{dr}\cdot\frac{dr}{dt}=4\pi r^{2}\frac{dr}{dt}$$

**Step 3 — solve for $\dfrac{dr}{dt}$:**

$$\frac{dr}{dt}=\frac{1}{4\pi r^{2}}\cdot\frac{dV}{dt}=\frac{900}{4\pi r^{2}}=\frac{225}{\pi r^{2}}$$

**Step 4 — substitute $r=15$:**

$$\frac{dr}{dt}=\frac{225}{\pi(15)^{2}}=\frac{225}{225\pi}=\frac{1}{\pi}\ \text{cm/s}$$

$$\therefore\ \frac{dr}{dt}=\frac{1}{\pi}\approx0.318\ \text{cm/s}$$

**The radius is increasing at $\dfrac{1}{\pi}$ cm/s** (about $0.32$ cm/s) when $r=15$ cm. The rate falls as $r$ grows, since the same volume of gas is spread over a larger surface.

questions.question: Or, verify Rolle's theorem for the function $f(x)=x^{2}-4x+3$ in the interval $[1,3]$. / Or, find the value of $c$ of Rolle's theorem for $f(x)=x^{2}-4x+3$ in $[1,3]$.
questions.answer:
**Rolle's theorem** requires three conditions on $[a,b]$: (1) $f$ continuous on $[a,b]$, (2) $f$ differentiable on $(a,b)$, (3) $f(a)=f(b)$. Then there exists $c\in(a,b)$ with $f'(c)=0$.

**Check the conditions** for $f(x)=x^{2}-4x+3$ on $[1,3]$:

**(1)** $f$ is a polynomial, hence continuous on $[1,3]$ ✓

**(2)** $f'(x)=2x-4$, which exists for every $x$ in $(1,3)$ ✓

**(3)** $f(1)=1-4+3=0$ and $f(3)=9-12+3=0$, so $f(1)=f(3)=0$ ✓

All three conditions hold, so some $c\in(1,3)$ must satisfy $f'(c)=0$.

**Find that $c$:**

$$f'(c)=0\ \Rightarrow\ 2c-4=0\ \Rightarrow\ c=2$$

$$\therefore\ c=2\in(1,3)$$

Since $c=2$ lies in the open interval, Rolle's theorem is **verified**. (The point $(2,-1)$ is the vertex of the parabola — the one place where the tangent is horizontal.)

questions.question: Evaluate: $\displaystyle\int e^{x}\frac{(x-1)}{(x+1)^{3}}\,dx$. / Or, evaluate $\displaystyle\int e^{x}\left[\frac{x-1}{(x+1)^{3}}\right]dx$.
questions.answer:
Split the integrand so that one factor is the derivative of the rest:

$$I=\int e^{x}\frac{x-1}{(x+1)^{3}}dx$$

Write $\dfrac{x-1}{(x+1)^{3}}=\dfrac{(x+1)-2}{(x+1)^{3}}=\dfrac{1}{(x+1)^{2}}-\dfrac{2}{(x+1)^{3}}$:

$$I=\int e^{x}\left[\frac{1}{(x+1)^{2}}-\frac{2}{(x+1)^{3}}\right]dx$$

Now recognise a derivative. Let $u=\dfrac{1}{(x+1)^{2}}$. Then

$$\frac{du}{dx}=-2(x+1)^{-3}=\frac{-2}{(x+1)^{3}}$$

so the bracket is exactly $u+\dfrac{du}{dx}$. Hence

$$I=\int\left(e^{x}u+e^{x}\frac{du}{dx}\right)dx=\int\frac{d}{dx}\left(e^{x}u\right)dx=e^{x}u+C$$

$$\therefore\ I=\frac{e^{x}}{(x+1)^{2}}+C$$

**Check by differentiating:**

$$\frac{d}{dx}\frac{e^{x}}{(x+1)^{2}}=e^{x}(x+1)^{-2}-2e^{x}(x+1)^{-3}=\frac{e^{x}\left[(x+1)-2\right]}{(x+1)^{3}}=\frac{e^{x}(x-1)}{(x+1)^{3}}\ ✓$$

*Note on the printed key:* the booklet carries out a lengthy integration by parts and ends with $-\dfrac{e^{x}}{2(x+1)^{2}}\left(x^{2}-x-1\right)+C$, which does **not** differentiate back to the integrand (the residual is $\dfrac{e^x\left(-x^{3}-3x+2\right)}{2(x+1)^{3}}$). The correct primitive is $\dfrac{e^{x}}{(x+1)^{2}}+C$.

questions.question: Prove that $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi}\frac{x}{1+\sin x}\,dx=\pi$.
questions.answer:
Let

$$I=\int_0^{\pi}\frac{x}{1+\sin x}dx\qquad\ldots(1)$$

Use the property $\displaystyle\int_0^{a}f(x)dx=\int_0^{a}f(a-x)dx$ with $a=\pi$. Since $\sin(\pi-x)=\sin x$:

$$I=\int_0^{\pi}\frac{\pi-x}{1+\sin(\pi-x)}dx=\int_0^{\pi}\frac{\pi-x}{1+\sin x}dx\qquad\ldots(2)$$

Add (1) and (2):

$$2I=\int_0^{\pi}\frac{x+\pi-x}{1+\sin x}dx=\pi\int_0^{\pi}\frac{dx}{1+\sin x}$$

Now evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi}\frac{dx}{1+\sin x}$: multiply by $\dfrac{1-\sin x}{1-\sin x}$ so that the denominator becomes $1-\sin^2x=\cos^2x$:

$$\int_0^{\pi}\frac{1-\sin x}{\cos^{2}x}dx=\int_0^{\pi}\left(\sec^{2}x-\sec x\tan x\right)dx$$

$$=\left[\tan x-\sec x\right]_0^{\pi}=\left(0-(-1)\right)-\left(0-1\right)=1+1=2$$

Therefore

$$2I=\pi\cdot2\ \Rightarrow\ I=\pi$$

$$\therefore\ \int_0^{\pi}\frac{x}{1+\sin x}dx=\pi\qquad\blacksquare$$

*(Verified numerically: the integral is $3.14159\ldots=\pi$ ✓.)*

questions.topic: Definite Integral as Limit of a Sum
questions.question: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^{1}\left(x+x^{2}\right)dx$ as a limit of a sum.
questions.answer:
**Set-up.** Divide $[0,1]$ into $n$ equal sub-intervals of width $h=\dfrac{1-0}{n}=\dfrac1n$; the points are $x_r=rh$ for $r=0,1,\ldots,n$, and $f(x)=x+x^{2}$.

By the definition of a definite integral as a limit of a sum:

$$\int_0^1 f(x)dx=\lim_{n\to\infty}h\sum_{r=1}^{n}f(rh)=\lim_{n\to\infty}h\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(rh+r^{2}h^{2}\right)$$

**Evaluate the sum.** Using $\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{n}r=\frac{n(n+1)}{2}$ and $\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{n}r^{2}=\frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6}$:

$$h\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(rh+r^{2}h^{2}\right)=h^{2}\sum r+h^{3}\sum r^{2}$$

$$=h^{2}\cdot\frac{n(n+1)}{2}+h^{3}\cdot\frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6}$$

Substituting $h=\dfrac1n$:

$$=\frac{n(n+1)}{2n^{2}}+\frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6n^{3}}$$

$$=\frac12\left(1+\frac1n\right)+\frac16\left(1+\frac1n\right)\left(2+\frac1n\right)$$

**Take the limit** as $n\to\infty$ (so $\frac1n\to0$):

$$\int_0^1\left(x+x^{2}\right)dx=\frac12(1)+\frac16(1)(2)=\frac12+\frac13=\frac56$$

$$\therefore\ \int_0^{1}\left(x+x^{2}\right)dx=\frac56$$

*Note on the printed key:* the booklet evaluates the integral by the ordinary antiderivative formula, $\left[\frac{x^2}{2}+\frac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^1=\frac12+\frac13=\frac56$ — the **value is right**, but the question asks specifically for the *limit of a sum*, so the summation above is the method required for full credit.

questions.question: If $\vec a=2\hat i-\hat j+\hat k$ and $\vec b=\hat i+\hat j+\hat k$, then find: (i) $|\vec a|$ (ii) $\vec a\cdot\vec b$ (iii) $\vec a\times\vec b$ (iv) projection of $\vec b$ on $\vec a$.
questions.answer:
**(i) Magnitude:**

$$\left|\vec a\right|=\sqrt{2^{2}+(-1)^{2}+1^{2}}=\sqrt{4+1+1}=\sqrt6\approx2.449$$

**(ii) Dot product:**

$$\vec a\cdot\vec b=(2)(1)+(-1)(1)+(1)(1)=2-1+1=2$$

**(iii) Cross product:**

$$\vec a\times\vec b=\begin{vmatrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\ 2&-1&1\\ 1&1&1\end{vmatrix}$$

$$=\hat i\left[(-1)(1)-(1)(1)\right]-\hat j\left[(2)(1)-(1)(1)\right]+\hat k\left[(2)(1)-(-1)(1)\right]$$

$$=\hat i(-1-1)-\hat j(2-1)+\hat k(2+1)=-2\hat i-\hat j+3\hat k$$

**(iv) Projection of $\vec b$ on $\vec a$:**

$$\text{proj}_{\vec a}\vec b=\frac{\vec a\cdot\vec b}{\left|\vec a\right|}=\frac{2}{\sqrt6}=\frac{\sqrt6}{3}\approx0.816$$

Equivalently, the projection as a vector is $\dfrac{2}{6}\left(2\hat i-\hat j+\hat k\right)=\dfrac13\left(2\hat i-\hat j+\hat k\right)$, whose magnitude is $\dfrac{\sqrt6}{3}$ ✓.

*Note on the printed key:* the booklet writes $|\vec a|=\sqrt{2^{2}+1^{2}+1^{2}}=\sqrt4=2$ — with $4$ under the root instead of $6$ — and then quotes the projection as $\dfrac{1}{|\vec a|}(a\cdot b)=\dfrac12(2)=10$, which is arithmetically inconsistent. The correct values are $|\vec a|=\sqrt6$ and projection $=\dfrac{2}{\sqrt6}=\dfrac{\sqrt6}{3}$. Parts (ii) and (iii) as printed are correct.

questions.question: Find the value of $\lambda$ so that the four points with position vectors $-6\hat i+3\hat j+2\hat k$, $3\hat i+\lambda\hat j+4\hat k$, $5\hat i+7\hat j+3\hat k$ and $-13\hat i+17\hat j-2\hat k$ may be coplanar.
questions.answer:
Four points with position vectors $\vec A,\vec B,\vec C,\vec D$ are coplanar exactly when the three vectors from $A$ are linearly dependent:

$$\left[\vec{AB}\ \vec{AC}\ \vec{AD}\right]=\begin{vmatrix}\vec{AB}\\\vec{AC}\\\vec{AD}\end{vmatrix}=0$$

Take $\vec A=-6\hat i+3\hat j+2\hat k$ and form the differences:

$$\vec{AB}=(3+6)\hat i+(\lambda-3)\hat j+(4-2)\hat k=9\hat i+(\lambda-3)\hat j+2\hat k$$

$$\vec{AC}=(5+6)\hat i+(7-3)\hat j+(3-2)\hat k=11\hat i+4\hat j+\hat k$$

$$\vec{AD}=(-13+6)\hat i+(17-3)\hat j+(-2-2)\hat k=-7\hat i+14\hat j-4\hat k$$

Expand the determinant along the first row:

$$\begin{vmatrix}9&\lambda-3&2\\ 11&4&1\\ -7&14&-4\end{vmatrix}=9\left[(4)(-4)-(1)(14)\right]-(\lambda-3)\left[(11)(-4)-(1)(-7)\right]+2\left[(11)(14)-(4)(-7)\right]$$

$$=9(-16-14)-(\lambda-3)(-44+7)+2(154+28)$$

$$=9(-30)-(\lambda-3)(-37)+2(182)$$

$$=-270+37(\lambda-3)+364$$

$$=-270+37\lambda-111+364=37\lambda-17$$

Set this equal to zero:

$$37\lambda-17=0\ \Rightarrow\ \lambda=\frac{17}{37}$$

$$\therefore\ \lambda=\frac{17}{37}\approx0.4595$$

**Check:** with $\lambda=\frac{17}{37}$ the determinant is $37\cdot\frac{17}{37}-17=0$ ✓.

*Note on the printed key:* the booklet's cross-multiplication gives $\lambda=\dfrac{147}{9776}\approx0.0150$, which leaves the determinant at $\approx-16.44$, not zero. The value that makes the four points coplanar is $\dfrac{17}{37}$.

questions.question: Let A and B be two events such that $2P(A)=P(B)=\dfrac{5}{13}$ and $P(A/B)=\dfrac25$. Find $P(A\cup B)$.
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — separate the given relations.** $2P(A)=\dfrac{5}{13}$ gives

$$P(A)=\frac{5}{26}$$

and $P(B)=\dfrac{5}{13}=\dfrac{10}{26}$.

**Step 2 — find $P(A\cap B)$** from the definition of conditional probability:

$$P(A/B)=\frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}\ \Rightarrow\ P(A\cap B)=P(A/B)\cdot P(B)$$

$$P(A\cap B)=\frac25\cdot\frac{5}{13}=\frac{2}{13}=\frac{4}{26}$$

**Step 3 — addition theorem:**

$$P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)$$

$$=\frac{5}{26}+\frac{10}{26}-\frac{4}{26}=\frac{11}{26}$$

$$\therefore\ P(A\cup B)=\frac{11}{26}\approx0.423$$

(The result is consistent: $P(A\cup B)=\frac{11}{26}<1$, and it exceeds both $P(A)$ and $P(B)$ as it must.)

questions.question: Using elementary row transformation, find the inverse of matrix A where $A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2&3\\ 2&5&7\\ -2&-4&-5\end{bmatrix}$.
questions.answer:
Write $A$ beside the identity and reduce $A$ to $I$, applying each row operation to both sides; the right-hand block then becomes $A^{-1}$.

$$\left[\begin{array}{ccc|ccc}1&2&3&1&0&0\\ 2&5&7&0&1&0\\ -2&-4&-5&0&0&1\end{array}\right]$$

**$R_2\to R_2-2R_1$, $R_3\to R_3+2R_1$:**

$$\left[\begin{array}{ccc|ccc}1&2&3&1&0&0\\ 0&1&1&-2&1&0\\ 0&0&1&2&0&1\end{array}\right]$$

**$R_1\to R_1-3R_3$, $R_2\to R_2-R_3$:**

$$\left[\begin{array}{ccc|ccc}1&2&0&-5&0&-3\\ 0&1&0&-4&1&-1\\ 0&0&1&2&0&1\end{array}\right]$$

**$R_1\to R_1-2R_2$:**

$$\left[\begin{array}{ccc|ccc}1&0&0&3&-2&-1\\ 0&1&0&-4&1&-1\\ 0&0&1&2&0&1\end{array}\right]$$

$$\therefore\ A^{-1}=\begin{bmatrix}3&-2&-1\\ -4&1&-1\\ 2&0&1\end{bmatrix}$$

**Check ($AA^{-1}=I$), first row:**

$$(1)(3)+(2)(-4)+(3)(2)=3-8+6=1\ ✓$$

$$(1)(-2)+(2)(1)+(3)(0)=-2+2+0=0\ ✓$$

$$(1)(-1)+(2)(-1)+(3)(1)=-1-2+3=0\ ✓$$

The remaining rows check similarly, so the inverse is correct. (Note $|A|=1$, which is why the entries of $A^{-1}$ are integers.)

questions.question: **[Q28 — the question stem is not printed in the scanned copy; only its worked solution survives.]** The solution refers to three urns A, B and C, from one of which two balls are drawn: $P(E_1)=P(E_2)=P(E_3)=\frac13$; for urn C the probability of drawing one white and one red is $\frac{{}^{3}C_1\times{}^{3}C_1}{{}^{6}C_2}=\frac{12}{66}=\frac{2}{11}$ (as printed); and for urn A it is $\frac{{}^{1}C_1\times{}^{3}C_1}{{}^{6}C_2}=\frac{3}{15}=\frac15$ (as printed). The question asks for the probability that the two balls drawn are one white and one red.
questions.answer:
**Situation reconstructed strictly from the printed solution.** There are three urns $A$, $B$, $C$, and the urn is chosen at random, so the prior probabilities are

$$P(E_1)=P(E_2)=P(E_3)=\frac13$$

where $E_1,E_2,E_3$ denote 'balls drawn from urn A / B / C'. Two balls are drawn from the chosen urn, and $E$ is the event 'one white and one red'.

**Step 1 — conditional probabilities** by counting favourable pairs out of all pairs:

$$P(E/E_1)=\frac{{}^{1}C_1\times{}^{3}C_1}{{}^{6}C_2}=\frac{1\times3}{15}=\frac15$$

$$P(E/E_3)=\frac{{}^{3}C_1\times{}^{3}C_1}{{}^{6}C_2}$$

**Step 2 — the total probability theorem:**

$$P(E)=P(E_1)P(E/E_1)+P(E_2)P(E/E_2)+P(E_3)P(E/E_3)$$

$$=\frac13\left[\frac15+P(E/E_2)+\frac{9}{15}\right]$$

$$=\frac13\left[\frac{10}{15}+P(E/E_2)\right]$$

with $P(E/E_2)$ read off from urn B's composition in the same way.

**The method is what matters here** and it is fully shown: (i) list the prior probabilities $\frac13$ for each urn, (ii) compute each conditional probability by ${}^{w}C_1\times{}^{r}C_1\big/{}^{w+r}C_2$, (iii) combine them with the total probability theorem.

*Note on the printed key:* the booklet prints $\dfrac{{}^{3}C_1\times{}^{3}C_1}{{}^{6}C_2}=\dfrac{12}{66}=\dfrac{2}{11}$ — but ${}^{6}C_2=15$, not $66$ (and $9/15=\frac35$, not $\frac{2}{11}$); the denominator $66={}^{12}C_2$ belongs to a 12-ball urn. The counting *method* printed is right, the arithmetic is not, so the final numerical answer cannot be trusted. The general working above is the reliable guide.

questions.question: Solve graphically the following L.P.P.: Minimise $Z=-3x+4y$ subject to $x+2y\le8$, $3x+2y\le12$ and $x,y\ge0$.
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — convert each constraint to a line.**

**Line 1:** $x+2y=8$ meets the axes at $(8,0)$ and $(0,4)$. Checking the origin, $0+0=0\le8$ ✓, so the feasible side contains $O$.

**Line 2:** $3x+2y=12$ meets the axes at $(4,0)$ and $(0,6)$. Checking the origin, $0\le12$ ✓, so again the side containing $O$ is feasible.

Together with $x\ge0,\ y\ge0$, the feasible region is the closed quadrilateral with vertices

$$O(0,0),\qquad A(4,0),\qquad B(0,4)$$

and the intersection of the two lines.

**Step 2 — the intersection point.** Solve simultaneously:

$$x+2y=8,\qquad 3x+2y=12$$

Subtracting: $2x=4$, so $x=2$, and then $2+2y=8$ gives $y=3$. So

$$B(2,3)$$

Rename the vertices $O(0,0)$, $A(4,0)$, $B(2,3)$, $C(0,4)$ — the region is the quadrilateral $OABC$.

**Step 3 — evaluate $Z=-3x+4y$ at each vertex:**

| Vertex | $Z=-3x+4y$ |
|---|---|
| $O(0,0)$ | $0$ |
| $A(4,0)$ | $-3(4)+4(0)=-12$ |
| $B(2,3)$ | $-3(2)+4(3)=6$ |
| $C(0,4)$ | $-3(0)+4(4)=16$ |

**Step 4 — conclusion.**

$$Z_{\min}=-12\ \text{at}\ (x,y)=(4,0),\qquad Z_{\max}=16\ \text{at}\ (x,y)=(0,4)$$

The question asks for the **minimum**:

$$\therefore\ Z_{\min}=-12\quad\text{at}\quad x=4,\ y=0$$

*(All four vertices were checked against both inequalities: $A(4,0)$ gives $4\le8$ and $12\le12$ ✓; $B(2,3)$ gives $8\le8$ and $12\le12$ ✓; $C(0,4)$ gives $8\le8$ and $8\le12$ ✓. Since $Z$ is linear, the extreme values occur at vertices.)*
